newsitem.title: UK: BOE seen holding fire on UK rates after pay data.
newsitem.headline: BOE seen holding fire on UK rates after pay data.

text.p: The unexpected slowing in May average earnings growth to an underlying 4.25 percent from 4.5 should help convince the Bank of England not to impose the fourth UK rate rise in as many months, analysts say.
"The average earnings numbers have increased the chances that the next rise in interest rates will be September rather than August," said Lehman Brothers UK economist Michael Dicks.

The next meeting of the central bank's interest rate setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is set for August 6 and 7 and there had been speculation interest rates could rise by another 25 basis points, taking them to 7.0 percent.
British official rates have risen by three times since May as the authorities try to prevent the exuberant consumer sector from pushing the economy into an unsustainable boom.
Given the persistent worries over personal sector spending, analysts say that Wednesday's June retail sales data are likely to have the final say on the timing of any further rate rise.
"If we see a soft number there, it really might persuade them to hang fire," Dicks said.

HSBC economist Dharshini David took a similar view. "I think the average earnings numbers could delay the rate rise until September but it depends on the retail sales figures. They could blow everything else out of the water," David said.

But she also argued that it was possible that the June retail sales data might be distorted by wet weather that month which could have persuaded shoppers to stay at home. This could lead to a strong figure as a reaction for July, paving the way for higher rates in September.
"We expect another quarter point rise in September and one more before the end of the year to take us to 7.25 percent," David said.
The Bank of England underlined its concerns about the recent strength of earnings, in the minutes of the inaugural meeting of its MPC on June 5 and 6, also published on Wednesday.
It said members of the committee viewed the gradual rise in real average earnings growth since late 1995 as evidence of tightening in the British labour market.

But the central bank's staff had revised down their estimates of underlying average earnings growth, excluding the effects of bonus payments, slightly downwards to 4.25/4.5 percent from 4.5 percent, following a downward revision to official figures for March.

Analysts said the central bank was therefore likely to welcome the latest reduction in the growth rate but they caution that there are significant problems with the average earnings data series, which may prevent it from carrying too much weight.

Moreover, the unexpectedly sharp reduction in seasonally adjusted unemployment benefit claimant figures for June -- down 36,500 compared with expectations of a 25,000 drop -- has also highlighted the increasingly tight conditions in the labour market.

"Earnings growth could well stop them from tightening at the August meeting, but the continuing reduction in unemployment does put inflationary pressure on average earnings," Royal Bank of Scotland economist Neil Parker said.

The Office for National Statistics says that the unemployment series is now free of the distorting effects of changes in benefit criteria but some analysts take the view that the data might still be understating the extent of unemployment.

"The Labour Force Survey unemployment rate at 7.2 percent, gives us a more accurate measure of spare capacity in the labour market, and suggests a trend fall of 25,000 per month," said NatWest markets economist John O'Sullivan.
The claimant unemployment rate, by contrast, dipped to 5.7 percent in June, from 5.8 percent in May, and was the lowest rate since August 1990.
Analysts expressed some concern about May unit wage costs, with the three-monthly annual growth rate accelerating to 2.4 percent from April's 2.1 percent.

"The worry is with manufacturing continuing to be depressed by sterling strength, we may have seen the best news of wage costs, and in months to come wage costs could continue to head higher unless manufacturers shed a great deal of labour," Schroders UK economist David Philpotts said.
The September MPC meeting is scheduled for September 10 and 11, with the announcement of the interest rate decision due on the second day.
--Cheryl Juckes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109
